messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bounpheng is a 77-year-old retired firefighter who has been married to his wife, Malee, for over fifty years. He was brought to the clinic at her gentle insistence after an incident last month when a neighbor’s fireworks display left him huddled in their basement, unable to speak, for several hours. For most of his life, Bounpheng managed, but in the quiet of retirement, the past has become louder than the present. The trauma dates back to his youth in Laos, decades before he became a firefighter known for his calm under pressure. He was a teenager selling fruit with two friends in a bustling open-air market when an unmarked plane flew overhead. The first explosion threw him against a wall, the world dissolving into a roar of sound and dust. When he could see again, the market was gone, replaced by craters and screams. His friends were dead. He remembers the surreal silence that followed the noise, the arrival of a single, siren-less emergency vehicle, and the feeling of being not a person, but a thing—an object left behind amidst the wreckage.

The sounds of his quiet suburban neighborhood have become a minefield. A car backfiring on the street is never just a car; it is the crack of the world splitting open. The sudden, percussive sound instantly triggers a cascade of vivid images from that day in the market (*Triggers → Memory*). The memories are not faded; they are sharp, sensory fragments that force their way into his mind, unwanted and unstoppable. He sees his friends’ faces, he smells the dust and smoke, and he feels the same profound helplessness that paralyzed him then. With these images comes the crushing weight of his own judgment: a better man would have seen the danger, a different person would have done something to help them (*Memory → Negative Appraisals*). He has come to believe that his survival was a fluke of his own inadequacy. The trigger doesn't just bring back the event; it brings back his interpretation of himself as a failure and an object (*Triggers → Negative Appraisals*).

This profound sense of being broken and unable to cope governs his days. Bounpheng is certain that if he were to truly let himself think about the event, to sit with the memories, he would completely lose control (*Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance*). This core belief fuels a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. In response to his appraisals of weakness, he spends hours at his front window, not admiring the garden but scanning the street, tracking every car and pedestrian, searching for anything out of place (*Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies*). It is a self-imposed watch he feels he must maintain. Even hearing a name similar to one of his fallen friends on the television news can send him into this heightened state of alert, forcing him to get up and check that all the doors are locked (*Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies*). His internal sense of threat makes him perpetually scan his environment for the external proof he is certain he will find (*Negative Appraisals → Triggers*).

The memories themselves feel like an alien presence. He describes them as being like a film of someone else’s life, a foolish boy he barely recognizes, which makes the vividness all the more disturbing (*Memory: Feels Alien*). When these intrusive memories surface, especially at night, his immediate response is to act. He will get out of bed and begin pacing the house, turning on lights, or retreat to the garage to lose himself in imagined scenarios of finding and punishing the men responsible for the bombing (*Memory → Maladaptive Strategies*). Yet this deliberate agitation, this attempt to regain control through fantasy and movement, only seems to keep the trauma active in his mind, ensuring the intrusive images return with greater frequency (*Maladaptive Strategies → Memory*).

Over the years, these behaviors have calcified into a rigid and isolating routine. The dark is the most potent trigger, so he avoids sleep for as long as he can, often dozing in his armchair with the television on until dawn. Malee now sleeps alone most nights. The chronic exhaustion from this avoidance only reinforces his belief that he is weak and deteriorating, a fragile man who could not possibly handle a direct confrontation with his past (*Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals*). The cycle is relentless: the trigger, the memory, the negative appraisal, and the maladaptive strategy all feed one another, a closed loop that has shrunk his world to the four walls of his house. He has come to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet dread, convinced he is being asked to do the one thing he cannot: remember. He is terrified that talking about the boy in the market will finally prove that he is nothing more than the object he has felt like for sixty years.
